entry.title: Coupled-perturbed Hartree-Fock equations
entry.content:
The coupled-perturbed Hartree-Fock (CPHF) equations are used to solve the response of molecular orbitals to each external perturbation (the \(U^x\) matrices below). Before working on the derivations, it is worth noting that the CPHF equations are not explicitly solved for first-order energy derivatives (i.e., gradients) in quantum chemistry. Please see the comments at the end of this note for details.

The Hartree-Fock (or density functional theory) eigenvalue-equations remain true in the presence of external perturbations \(x\), i.e.,

\[F^{AO}(x)C(x)=S^{AO}(x)C(x)E(x)\]

The unperturbed coefficients \(C(0)\) represent the unperturbed molecular orbitals \(\phi_p(0)=\sum_\mu C_{\mu p}(0)f_\mu\), where \(f_\mu\) are the atomic orbitals. With perturbation, the molecular orbitals can be expanded in the basis of unperturbed molecular orbitals

\[\phi_p(x)=\sum_{q}U_{qp}(x)\phi_q(0)=\sum_{\mu}\sum_{q}U_{qp}(x)C_{\mu q}(0)f_\mu\]

It is obvious that the perturbed coefficients \(C(x)\) can be written as

\[C(x)=C(0)U(x)\]

With defining \(F(x)\equiv C^\dagger(0)F^{AO}C(0)\) and \(S(x)\equiv C^\dagger(0)S^{AO}C(0)\), we have \(F(0)=E(0)\), \(U(0)=S(0)=I\), and

\[F(x)U(x)=S(x)U(x)E(x)\]

as well as the orthonormality condition

\[U^\dagger(x)S(x)U(x)=I\]

Evaluate the derivatives of the above equations with respect to \(x\) at \(x=0\), use the notation \(O^x\equiv rac{\partial O}{\partial x}\), and we have

\[F^x(0)+E(0)U^x(0)=S^x(0)E(0) + U^x(0)E(0) + E^x(0)\] \[U^{\dagger x}(0) + U^x(0) = - S^x(0)\]

Ommiting the \(0\), we have the following equations

\[F^x_{pq} +E_pU^x_{pq} = S^x_{pq}E_q + U^x_{pq}E_q + E^x_{p}\delta_{pq}\] \[U^{x \ast}_{qp} + U^x_{pq} = - S^x_{pq}\]

for \(p=q\)

\[Re[U^x_{pp}] = - rac{1}{2}S^x_{pp}\]

for \(p eq q\)

\[U^x_{pq} = rac{F^x_{pq}-S^x_{pq}E_q}{E_q-E_p}\]

To solve \(U^x\), we have to know \(F^x\) and \(S^x\). The latter is easier and can be obtained as \(S^x(0)=C^\dagger(0) S^{AO,x} C(0)\). For Fock operator, we have

\[ egin{gathered} F_{pq}(x)=\sum_{\mu u}C_{\mu p}^{*}(0)C_{ u q}(0)\left[h_{\mu u}(x)+\sum_{i ho\sigma}C_{ ho i}^{*}(x)C_{\sigma i}(x)\langle\mu ho|| u\sigma angle(x) ight] \ =\sum_{\mu u}C_{\mu p}^{*}(0)C_{ u q}(0)\left[h_{\mu u}(x)+\sum_{i ho\sigma}\sum_{ts}C_{ ho t}^{*}(0)U_{ti}^{*}(x) C_{\sigma s}(0)U_{si}(x)\langle\mu ho|| u\sigma angle(x) ight] \ =h_{pq}(x)+\sum_{i}\sum_{ts}U_{ti}^{*}(x)U_{si}(x)\langle pt||qs angle(x) \end{gathered}\] \[ egin{gathered} F_{pq}^{x}=h_{pq}^{x}(0)+\sum_{i}\left[\langle pi||qi angle^{x}(0)+\sum_{t}U_{ti}^{x*}(0)\langle pt||qi angle(0)+\sum_{s}U_{si}^{x}(0)\langle pi||qs angle(0) ight] \ =f_{pq}^{x}+\sum_{it}[U_{ti}^{x*}\langle pt||qi angle+U_{ti}^{x}\langle pi||qt angle] \ =f_{pq}^{x}+\sum_{ij} igl[U_{ji}^{x*}\langle pj||qi angle+U_{ji}^{x}\langle pi||qj angle igr]+\sum_{ia} igl[U_{ai}^{x*}\langle pa||qi angle+U_{ai}^{x}\langle pi||qa angle igr] \ =f_{pq}^{x}-\sum_{ij}S_{ij}^{x}\langle pj||qi angle+\sum_{ia}[U_{ai}^{x*}\langle pa||qi angle+U_{ai}^{x}\langle pi||qa angle] \end{gathered}\]

As a result, we have

\[U_{pq}^x= rac{G_{pq}+\sum_{ia}[U_{ai}^{x*}\langle pa||qi angle+U_{ai}^x\langle pi||qa angle]}{E_q-E_p}\]

where

\[G_{pq}=f_{pq}^x-S_{pq}^xE_q-\sum_{ij}S_{ij}^x\langle pj||qi angle\]

We note that these equations are coupled only for \(U^x_{ai}\) block. After solving \(U^x_{ai}\), all the other blocks can be calculated without any iteration. The CPHF equations for \(U^x_{ai}\) can be reformulated as

\[ egin{bmatrix}\Delta+A&B\B^*&\Delta+A^*\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix}U^x\U^{x*}\end{bmatrix}=- egin{bmatrix}G^x\G^{x*}\end{bmatrix}\]

where

\[\Delta_{bj,ai}= igl(E_{b}-E_{j} igr)\delta_{ba}\delta_{ji}\] \[A_{bj,ai}=\langle bi||ja angle, B_{bj,ai}=\langle ba||ji angle\]

One can see that the CPHF equation has to be solved for each perturbation (or each \(x\)) independently and this would be computationally expensive.

But as we mentioned before, the CPHF equations are not explicitly solved for first-order energy derivatives. This is consistent with the famous “2n+1” rule that to calculate the 2n+1 order property, one only needs to solve the n order response of the wave function. In practice, one can show that to calculate the first-order energy derivatives, one only needs to solve the contributions with the following form

\[\sum_{ia}\left(U_{ai}^{x}I_{ai}^\ast+U_{ai}^{x\ast}I_{ai} ight)\]

It can be reformulated as

\[\left[ egin{array}{cc}I^*&I\end{array} ight]\left[ egin{array}{c}U^x\U^{x*}\end{array} ight]=-\left[ egin{array}{cc}I^*&I\end{array} ight]\left[ egin{array}{cc}\Delta+A&B\B^*&\Delta+A^*\end{array} ight]^{-1}\left[ egin{array}{c}G^x\G^{x*}\end{array} ight]\]

If we can solve the following equation to obtain \(D\) intermediates

\[\left[ egin{array}{cc}D^* & D\end{array} ight]\left[ egin{array}{c}\Delta+A&B\B^*&\Delta+A^*\end{array} ight]=-\left[ egin{array}{cc}I^* & I\end{array} ight]\]

the original contributions can be written as

\[\sum_{ia}\left(U_{ai}^{x}I_{ai}^\ast+U_{ai}^{x\ast}I_{ai} ight) = \sum_{ia}\left(G_{ai}^{x}D_{ai}^\ast+G_{ai}^{x\ast}D_{ai} ight)\]

This is so-called “Z-vector” method in quantum chemistry. We emphasize that the Z-vector equations to solve \(D\) intermediates are perturbation-independent. It only needs to be solved once and can be used to calculate any first-order energy derivatives.

entry.title: Analytical gradients for electron-correlation methods
entry.content:
We follow the notations in J. Chem. Phys. 154, 064110 (2021). In this note, we use \(ij\dots,ab\dots,pq\dots\) for correlated orbitals, \(i^{\prime}j^{\prime}\dots,a^{\prime}b^{\prime}\dots,p^{\prime}q^{\prime}\dots\) for frozen core and frozen virtual orbitals, and \(IJ\dots,AB\dots,PQ\dots\) for all orbitals. This derivation has explicitly considered complex-valued integrals and frozen core/virtual orbitals. From the definition of the \(I^\prime\) intermediates, we have assumed canonical HF orbitals.

Take coupled cluster (CC) methods as an example. We define the (symmetrized) unrelaxed CC density matrices as

\[D_{pq}=\langle\Psi_{HF}|(1+\Lambda)e^{-T}\left\{ a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q} ight\} _{c}e^{T}|\Psi_{HF} angle_{x=0}\] \[\Gamma_{pq,rs}=\langle\Psi_{HF}|(1+\Lambda)e^{-T}\left\{ a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}^{\dagger}a_{s}a_{r} ight\} _{c}e^{T}|\Psi_{HF} angle_{x=0}\] \[ ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}= rac{1}{2}\left(\Gamma_{pq,rs}+\Gamma_{rs,pq}^{\ast} ight)\]

where \(x\) is the external perturbation parameter, \(\Lambda\) is the de-excitation operators solved in the \(\Lambda\)-equations, and \(T\) is the cluster operator. The CC energy and the energy derivatives are

\[E = \sum_{pq}f_{pq} D_{pq} + rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs}\langle pq||rs angle ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\] \[ rac{dE}{dx}=\sum_{pq} rac{df_{pq}}{dx}D_{pq}+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs} rac{d\langle pq||rs angle}{dx} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\]

In fact, the energy expression is not limited to CC methods. The following derivations are also applicable to other electron-correlation methods as long as the energy can be calculated using one- and two-particle unrelaxed density matrices.

Define the orbital relaxation \(\phi_{p}(x)=\sum_{T}U_{Tp}\phi_{T}(0)\) , \( rac{d}{dx}\phi_{p}(x)=\sum_{T}U_{Tp}^{x}\phi_{T}(0)\), and the derivatives of integrals

\[h_{pq}^{x}=\sum_{\mu u}C_{\mu p}^{\ast} rac{dh_{\mu u}}{dx}C_{ u q}\]

and

\[\langle pq||rs angle^{x}=\sum_{\mu u ho\sigma} rac{d\langle\mu u||\sigma ho angle}{dx}C_{\mu p}^{\ast}C_{ u q}^{\ast}C_{\sigma r}C_{ ho s}\]

We thus have

\[ egin{gathered} rac{df_{pq}}{dx}= & rac{d}{dx}\left(h_{pq}+\sum_{I}\langle pI||qI angle ight)=h_{pq}^{x}+\sum_{T}\left(U_{Tp}^{x\ast}h_{tq}+U_{Tq}h_{pt} ight)\ + & \sum_{I}\langle pI||rI angle^{x}+\sum_{TI}\left(U_{Tp}^{x\ast}\langle TI||qI angle+U_{Tq}\langle pI||TI angle+U_{TI}^{x\ast}\langle pT||qI angle+U_{TI}\langle pI||qT angle ight)\ = & f_{pq}^{x}+\sum_{T}\left(U_{Tp}^{x\ast}f_{Tq}+U_{Tq}f_{pT} ight)+\sum_{TI}\left(U_{TI}^{x\ast}\langle pT||qI angle+U_{TI}\langle pI||qT angle ight) \end{gathered}\]

and

\[ egin{gathered} rac{dE}{dx}= & \sum_{pq}D_{pq}f_{pq}^{x}+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs}\langle pq||rs angle^{x} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\ + & \sum_{pq}D_{pq}\left[\sum_{T}\left(U_{Tp}^{x\ast}f_{Tq}+U_{Tq}f_{pT} ight)+\sum_{TI}\left(U_{TI}^{x\ast}\langle pT||qI angle+U_{TI}\langle pI||qT angle ight) ight]\ + & rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\sum_{T}\left[U_{Tp}^{x\ast}\langle Tq||rs angle+U_{Tq}^{x\ast}\langle pT||rs angle+U_{Tr}^{x}\langle pq||Ts angle+U_{Ts}^{x}\langle pq||rT angle ight]\ \equiv & \left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{expectation}+\left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{relaxation} \end{gathered}\]

, where we define the expectation value and orbital relaxation part of the total energy derivative as

\[ egin{gathered}\left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{expectation}= & \sum_{pq}D_{pq}f_{pq}^{x}+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs}\langle pq||rs angle^{x} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\end{gathered}\] \[ egin{gathered}\left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{relaxation}= & \sum_{pq}D_{pq}\left[\sum_{T}\left(U_{Tp}^{x\ast}f_{tq}+U_{Tq}f_{pt} ight)+\sum_{TI}\left(U_{TI}^{x\ast}\langle pT||qI angle+U_{TI}\langle pI||qT angle ight) ight]\ + & rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\sum_{T}\left[U_{Tp}^{x\ast}\langle Tq||rs angle+U_{Tq}^{x\ast}\langle pT||rs angle+U_{Tr}^{x}\langle pq||Ts angle+U_{Ts}^{x}\langle pq||rT angle ight]\ = & \sum_{Tp}U_{Tp}^{x\ast}\sum_{q}D_{pq}f_{Tq}+\sum_{Tp}U_{Tp}^{x}\sum_{q}D_{qp}f_{qT}+\sum_{TI}U_{TI}^{x\ast}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pT||qI angle+\sum_{TI}U_{TI}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pI||qT angle\ + & rac{1}{4}\sum_{Tp}U_{Tp}^{x\ast}\sum_{qrs}\left[\langle Tq||rs angle ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}+\langle qT||rs angle ilde{\Gamma}_{qp,rs} ight]+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{Tr}U_{Tr}^{x}\sum_{pqs}\left[ ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\langle pq||Ts angle+ ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,sr}\langle pq||sT angle ight]\ = & \sum_{Tp}U_{Tp}^{x\ast}\sum_{q}D_{pq}f_{Tq}+\sum_{Tp}U_{Tp}^{x}\sum_{q}D_{qp}f_{qT}+\sum_{TI}U_{TI}^{x\ast}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pT||qI angle+\sum_{TI}U_{TI}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pI||qT angle\ + & rac{1}{2}\sum_{Tp}U_{Tp}^{x\ast}\sum_{qrs} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\langle Tq||rs angle+ rac{1}{2}\sum_{Tp}U_{Tp}^{x}\sum_{qrs} ilde{\Gamma}_{rs,pq}\langle rs||Tq angle \end{gathered}\]

For orbital relaxation, recall that

\[ egin{gathered} & \sum_{TI}U_{TI}^{x\ast}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pT||qI angle+\sum_{TI}U_{TI}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pI||qT angle\ = & \sum_{AI}U_{AI}^{x\ast}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pA||qI angle+\sum_{AI}U_{AI}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pI||qA angle\ + & \sum_{JI}U_{JI}^{x\ast}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pJ||qI angle+\sum_{IJ}U_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pJ||qI angle\ = & -\sum_{IJ}S_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pJ||qI angle+\sum_{AI}U_{AI}^{x\ast}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pA||qI angle+\sum_{AI}U_{AI}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pI||qA angle \end{gathered}\]

In the last step, we use the normalization condition (see CPHF equations)

\[U^{x \ast}_{qp} + U^x_{pq} = - S^x_{pq}\]

for the frozen core orbitals. The orbital relaxation part of the total energy derivative can be further simplified as

\[\left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{relaxation}=\left(\sum_{TP}U_{TP}^{x\ast}I_{TP}^{\prime}+c.c. ight)-\sum_{IJ}S_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{pq}D_{pq}\langle pJ||qI angle\]

where we have defined the \(I^\prime\) intermediates. If we assume canonical HF orbitals, i.e.,

\[ rac{dE}{dx}=\sum_{a} rac{df_{aa}}{dx}D_{aa}+\sum_{i} rac{df_{ii}}{dx}D_{ii}+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs} rac{d\langle pq||rs angle}{dx} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\]

, the non-zero blocks of \(I^\prime\) intermediates are

\[I_{tp}^{\prime}=\delta_{tp}D_{tt}f_{tt}+ rac{1}{2}\sum_{qrs} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\langle tq||rs angle+\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle rt||rp angle\delta_{ta}\delta_{pi}\] \[I_{a^{\prime}p}^{\prime}= rac{1}{2}\sum_{qrs} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\langle a^{\prime}q||rs angle+\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle ra^{\prime}||rp angle\delta_{pi}\] \[I_{i^{\prime}p}^{\prime}= rac{1}{2}\sum_{qrs} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}\langle i^{\prime}q||rs angle\] \[I_{Ai^{\prime}}^{\prime}=\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle rA||ri^{\prime} angle\]

and

\[\left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{relaxation}=\left(\sum_{TP}U_{TP}^{x\ast}I_{TP}^{\prime}+c.c. ight)-\sum_{IJ}S_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle rJ||rI angle\]

To eliminate the \(U^x_{ia}\) terms and arrive at the Z-vector equation, we use the following relation

\[U_{ia}^{x\ast}=-S_{ai}^{x}-U_{ai}^{x},U_{i^{\prime}a}^{x\ast}=-S_{ai^{\prime}}^{x}-U_{ai^{\prime}}^{x}\] \[ egin{gathered}\sum_{TP}U_{TP}^{x\ast}I_{TP}^{\prime}+c.c.= & \sum_{other}U_{TP}^{x\ast}I_{TP}^{\prime}+c.c.+\sum_{ia}\left(-S_{ai}^{x}-U_{ai}^{x} ight)I_{ia}^{\prime}+\sum_{i^{\prime}a}\left(-S_{ai^{\prime}}^{x}-U_{ai^{\prime}}^{x} ight)I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime}+c.c.\ = & \sum_{other}U_{TP}^{x\ast}I_{TP}^{\prime}+c.c.+\sum_{ia}\left(-S_{ai}^{x}I_{ia}^{\prime}-U_{ai}^{x\ast}I_{ia}^{\prime\ast} ight)+\sum_{i^{\prime}a}\left(-S_{ai^{\prime}}^{x}I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime}-U_{ai^{\prime}}^{x\ast}I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime\ast} ight)+c.c \end{gathered}\]

By defining

\[I_{ai}^{\prime\prime}=I_{ai}^{\prime}-I_{ia}^{\prime\ast},I_{ai^{\prime}}^{\prime\prime}=I_{ai^{\prime}}^{\prime}-I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime\ast},I_{ia}^{\prime\prime}=I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime\prime}=0\]

and

\[I_{TP}^{\prime\prime}=I_{TP}^{\prime} ext{ for other cases},\] \[I_{PQ}^{\prime\prime}=0,PQ=ia,i^{\prime}a,i^{\prime}j^{\prime},ij^{\prime},Pa^{\prime},\]

we have

\[\left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{relaxation}=\left(\sum_{TP}U_{TP}^{x\ast}I_{TP}^{\prime\prime}+c.c. ight)-\sum_{IJ}S_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle rJ||rI angle-\left(\sum_{ia}S_{ai}^{x}I_{ia}^{\prime}+\sum_{i^{\prime}a}S_{ai^{\prime}}^{x}I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime}+c.c. ight)\]

Then we are able to write down the corresponding Z-vector equations as (see CPHF equations)

\[\left[ egin{array}{cc} D^{\prime\ast} & D^{\prime}\end{array} ight]\left[ egin{array}{cc} \Delta+A & B\ B^{\ast} & \Delta+A^{\ast} \end{array} ight]=-\left[ egin{array}{cc} I^{\prime\prime\ast} & I^{\prime\prime}\end{array} ight]\]

with

\[\Delta_{pq,rs}=(E_{p}-E_{q})\delta_{pr}\delta_{qs}\] \[A_{pq,ai}=\langle pi||qa angle\] \[B_{pq,ai}=\langle pa||qi angle\] \[G_{pq}^{x}\equiv f_{pq}^{x}-S_{pq}^{x}E_{q}-\sum_{ij}S_{ij}^{x}\langle pj||qi angle\]

By reformulating the Z-vector equations, we have (for\(P eq Q\))

\[D_{PQ}^{\prime}= rac{I_{PQ}^{\prime\prime}}{f_{QQ}-f_{PP}},PQ=ij,i^{\prime}j,ab,a^{\prime}b\] \[D_{PQ}^{\prime}=0,PQ=ia,i^{\prime}a,i^{\prime}j^{\prime},ij^{\prime},Pa^{\prime}\]

For the coupled AI-block, the Z-vector equations can be written as

\[\sum_{BJ}D_{BJ}^{\prime\ast}\langle BA||JI angle+\sum_{BJ}D_{BJ}^{\prime}\left[(F_{AA}-F_{II})\delta_{AB}\delta_{IJ}+\langle JA||BI angle ight]=-X_{AI}\]

where

\[X_{AI}=I_{AI}^{\prime\prime}+\sum_{PQ=ij,i^{\prime}j,ab,a^{\prime}b}\left[D_{PQ}^{\prime\ast}\langle PA||QI angle+D_{PQ}^{\prime}\langle QA||PI angle ight]\]

Finally, we have

\[ egin{gathered}\left\langle rac{dE}{dx} ight angle _{relaxation}= & \left(\sum_{TP}G_{TP}^{x\ast}D_{TP}^{\prime}+c.c. ight)+\sum_{p}D_{pp}f_{pp}^{x}+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs}\langle pq||rs angle^{x} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}-\sum_{IJ}S_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle rJ||rI angle\ - & \left(\sum_{ia}S_{ai}^{x}I_{ia}^{\prime}+\sum_{i^{\prime}a}S_{ai^{\prime}}^{x}I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime}+c.c. ight)\ = & \left(\sum_{TP}f_{PT}^{x}D_{TP}^{\prime}+c.c. ight)+\sum_{p}D_{pp}f_{pp}^{x}+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs}\langle pq||rs angle^{x} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}-\sum_{IJ}S_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle rJ||rI angle\ - & \left(\sum_{TP}S_{PT}^{x}f_{PP}D_{TP}^{\prime}+\sum_{IJ}S_{IJ}^{x}\sum_{TP}\langle PJ||TI angle D_{TP}^{\prime}+\sum_{ia}S_{ai}^{x}I_{ia}^{\prime}+\sum_{i^{\prime}a}S_{ai^{\prime}}^{x}I_{i^{\prime}a}^{\prime}+c.c. ight)\ \equiv & \sum_{PQ}\left(f_{PQ}^{x}D_{PQ}^{\prime\prime}+c.c. ight)+ rac{1}{4}\sum_{pqrs}\langle pq||rs angle^{x} ilde{\Gamma}_{pq,rs}+\sum_{PQ}\left(S_{PQ}^{x}I_{PQ}+c.c. ight) \end{gathered}\]

with

\[D_{PQ}^{\prime}=0,PQ=ia,i^{\prime}a,i^{\prime}j^{\prime},ij^{\prime},Pa^{\prime}\] \[D_{pq}^{\prime\prime}\equiv D_{qp}^{\prime}+ rac{1}{2}D_{pp}\delta_{pq}\] \[D_{PQ}^{\prime\prime}\equiv D_{QP}^{\prime} ext{, for other }PQ\] \[I_{IJ}=-D_{JI}^{\prime}f_{II}- rac{1}{2}\sum_{r}D_{rr}\langle rJ||rI angle-\sum_{TP}\langle PJ||TI angle D_{TP}^{\prime}\] \[I_{aI}=-I_{Ia}^{\prime}-D_{Ia}^{\prime}f_{aa}\] \[I_{PQ}=-D_{QP}^{\prime}f_{PP} ext{, for other }PQ\]

One last thing, the CPHF equation can only solve the response for non-degenerate orbitals (similar to non-degenerate perturbation theory). For degenerate (or identical) orbitals, we set the response \(U_{ii}^{\chi}=- rac{1}{2}S_{ii}^{\chi}\). This leads to extra terms for the \(I\) intermediates, i.e., if \(\epsilon_p = \epsilon_q\)

\[I_{pq}\leftarrow- rac{1}{2}I_{qp}^{\prime\prime}=- rac{1}{2}I_{qp}^{\prime}\]

The factor of 1/2 for the second term in \(I_{IJ}\) and the above contribution for degenerate orbitals are missing in the 2019 paper.

entry.title: Linear response thoery
entry.content:
Linear response (LR) theory relates the response of a molecular property to the excited states of the unperturbed system, or to a time-dependent external perturbation.

Assume we have solved the unperturbed electronic structure problem and obtained the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of unperturbed Hamiltonian

\[\hat{H}\Psi_n = E_n\Psi_n\]

Now apply the time dependent perturbation \(\hat{V}(t)\) to the system. The time-evolution of a specific state, e.g., the ground state \(\Psi_0\) can be described by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation

\[i\hbar rac{d}{dt}\Psi_0(t) = \left(\hat{H}+\hat{V}(t) ight)\Psi_0(t)\]

We can expand the time-dependent wavefunction as

\[\Psi_0(t) = \left(\Psi_0 + \delta\Psi_0(t) ight)e^{-iE_0t/\hbar}\]

The first-order response of wave function can be obtained by perturbation theory

\[\delta\Psi_0(t) = \sum_{n eq 0} c_n(t) \Psi_n\] \[i\hbar rac{d}{dt}c_n(t) = \langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(t) |\Psi_0 angle +\left( E_n - E_0 ight)c_n(t)\]

or equivalently

\[ egin{aligned} i\hbar c_n(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^t \left[\langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(t') |\Psi_0 angle +\left( E_n - E_0 ight)c_n(t') ight] dt'\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} heta(t-t')\left[\langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(t') |\Psi_0 angle +\left( E_n - E_0 ight)c_n(t') ight] dt' \end{aligned}\]

where \( heta(t-t')\) is the Heaviside step function. By using the Fourier transformation convolution theorem, we can obtain the response of the wave function in the frequency domain

\[ egin{aligned} i\hbar c_n(\omega) &= heta(\omega)\left[\langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(\omega) |\Psi_0 angle +\hbar\omega_{n0}c_n(\omega) ight] \ c_n(\omega) &= rac{\langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(\omega) |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega-\omega_{n0})} \ |\delta\Psi_0(\omega) angle &= \sum_{n eq 0} rac{\langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(\omega) |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega-\omega_{n0})} |\Psi_n angle \end{aligned}\]

where \(\omega_{n0} = (E_n - E_0)/\hbar\). In above equations, we have used that the Fourier transformation of the Heaviside step function \( heta(\omega) = \lim_{\epsilon ightarrow 0^+} rac{i}{\omega + i\epsilon}\).

Now consider the frequency-domain response of a molecular property, i.e., the expectation value of an operator \(\hat{a}\), to the perturbation

\[ egin{aligned} \langle \delta\hat{a}(\omega) angle & \equiv \langle \Psi_0(\omega) | \hat{a} |\Psi_0(\omega) angle - \langle \Psi_0 | \hat{a} |\Psi_0 angle \ & = \sum_{n eq 0} rac{\langle \Psi_0 | \hat{a} |\Psi_n angle\langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(\omega) |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega-\omega_{n0})} + ext{c.c.} \end{aligned}\]

If the perturbation is a time-dependent monochromatic electric field,

\[\hat{V}(t) = \hat{b}\cos(\omega_0 t) = rac{\hat{b}}{2}(e^{i\omega_0 t} + e^{-i\omega_0 t}) ,\] \[\hat{V}(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{i\omega t} \hat{V}(t) dt = \pi \hat{b} \left[ \delta(\omega+\omega_0) + \delta(\omega-\omega_0) ight]\]

we can obtain the linear response of any property \(\hat{a}\) to the electric field

\[ egin{aligned} \langle \delta\hat{a}(t) angle &= rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \sum_{n eq 0} rac{\langle \Psi_0 | \hat{a} |\Psi_n angle\langle \Psi_n | \hat{V}(\omega) |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega-\omega_{n0})} d\omega + ext{c.c.} \ &= rac{1}{2} \sum_{n eq 0} rac{\langle \Psi_0 | \hat{a} |\Psi_n angle\langle \Psi_n | \hat{b} |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega_0-\omega_{n0})} e^{-i\omega_0 t} \ &- rac{1}{2} \sum_{n eq 0} rac{\langle \Psi_0 | \hat{a} |\Psi_n angle\langle \Psi_n | \hat{b} |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega_0+\omega_{n0})} e^{i\omega_0 t} + ext{c.c.} \ & = \sum_{n eq 0} rac{\langle \Psi_0 | \hat{a} |\Psi_n angle\langle \Psi_n | \hat{b} |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega_0^2-\omega_{n0}^2)} \omega_{n0} \cos(\omega_0 t) \ & - i \sum_{n eq 0} rac{\langle \Psi_0 | \hat{a} |\Psi_n angle\langle \Psi_n | \hat{b} |\Psi_0 angle}{\hbar(\omega_0^2-\omega_{n0}^2)} \omega_0 \sin(\omega_0 t) + ext{c.c.} \end{aligned}\]

This result is very important, indicating the response of molecular properties is at the same frequency as the external perturbation \(\omega_0\).
entry.summary: Linear response (LR) theory relates the response of a molecular property to the excited states of the unperturbed system, or to a time-dependent external perturbation.

entry.title: Time-dependent Hartree-Fock method (response of density matrices)

link.title: Time-dependent Hartree-Fock method (response of density matrices)

entry.content:
There are many different ways to derive the linear response time-dependent HF (LR-TDHF) or LR-TDDFT equation. This derivation is based on the linear response of HF density matrices to an external perturbation following the derivations in the famous paper. The perturbation and the response of density matrices have the same form (same frequency) based on the linear response theory.

For any single-electron wave function, the time-dependent Schrödinger equation can be written as

\[i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}|\phi_{p}\rangle=\hat{f}(t)|\phi_{p}\rangle\]

If we expand \(\phi_{p}\) with a set of time-independent basis functions \(\{|\mu\rangle\}\), we have

\[\sum_{\mu}i\hbar|\mu\rangle\frac{\partial}{\partial t}c_{\mu p}(t)=\sum_{\mu}\hat{f}(t)c_{\mu p}(t)|\mu\rangle\]

Left project basis function and we have

\[i\hbar SC^{\prime}(t)=F(t)C(t)\]

and its complex conjugate

\[-i\hbar C^{^{\dagger}\prime}(t)S=C^{^{\dagger}}(t)F(t)\]

We have

\[\begin{aligned}i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}D(t)=i\hbar\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}C(t)\tilde{I}C^{\dagger}(t)\right)= & i\hbar\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}C(t)\right)\tilde{I}C^{\dagger}(t)+i\hbar C(t)\tilde{I}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}C^{\dagger}(t)\right)\\ = & S^{-1}F(t)D(t)-D(t)F(t)S^{-1} \end{aligned}\]

For a given orthonormal basis set, e.g., the unperturbed single-electron wave function, we have (in a.u.)

\[i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}D(t)=\left[F(t),D(t)\right]\]

Expand the above equation with perturbation series.

\[D(t) =D^{(0)}+D^{(1)}(t)+\cdots\] \[F(t) =F^{(0)}+F^{(1)}(t)+\cdots\]

and collect the first-order terms

\[i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}D^{(1)}(t)=F^{(0)}D^{(1)}(t)+F^{(1)}(t)D^{(0)}-D^{(0)}F^{(1)}(t)-D^{(1)}(t)F^{(0)}\]

With the perturbation Hamiltonian and the response of density matrices written in frequency-domain

\[g_{pq}=\frac{1}{2}\left[f_{pq}e^{-i\omega t}+f_{qp}^{*}e^{i\omega t}\right]\] \[D_{pq}^{(1)}=\frac{1}{2}\left[d_{pq}e^{-i\omega t}+d_{qp}^{*}e^{i\omega t}\right]\]

We note that \(F^{(1)}\neq g\) since it has another first-order contribution from the two-electron interaction.

\[F_{pq}^{(1)}=g_{pq}+\sum_{rs}\langle pr||qs\rangle D_{rs}^{(1)}\]

Collect the terms with \(e^{-i\omega t}\)

\[\begin{aligned}\omega d_{pq}= & \sum_{r}F_{pr}^{(0)}d_{rq}+\sum_{r}\left[f_{pr}+\sum_{mn}\langle pm||rn\rangle d_{mn}\right]D_{rq}^{(0)}\\ - & \sum_{r}d_{pr}F_{rq}^{(0)}-\sum_{r}D_{pr}^{(0)}\left[f_{rq}+\sum_{mn}\langle rm||qn\rangle d_{mn}\right] \end{aligned}\]

Noticing that \(DD=C\tilde{I}C^{\dagger}C\tilde{I}C^{\dagger}=D\), we have

\[D^{(0)}D^{(1)}+D^{(1)}D^{(0)}=D^{(1)}\]

with canonical orbitals, \(F_{pq}^{(0)}=\epsilon_{p}\delta_{pq},D_{pq}^{(0)}=\delta_{pq}\delta_{pi}\). We thus have the following restrictions on \(D^{(1)}\)

\[\left[\begin{array}{cc} D_{ii}^{(1)} & D_{ia}^{(1)}\\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{cc} D_{ii}^{(1)} & 0\\ D_{ai}^{(1)} & 0 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc} D_{ii}^{(1)} & D_{ia}^{(1)}\\ D_{ai}^{(1)} & D_{aa}^{(1)} \end{array}\right]\]

As a result, we can only have non-zero \(D_{ai}^{(1)}\) and \(D_{ia}^{(1)}\).

\[\omega d_{ai}=\left(\epsilon_{a}-\epsilon_{i}\right)d_{ai}+f_{ai}+\sum_{bj}\langle ab||ij\rangle d_{jb}+\sum_{bj}\langle aj||ib\rangle d_{bj}\] \[\omega d_{ia}=\left(\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{a}\right)d_{ia}-f_{ia}-\sum_{bj}\langle ib||aj\rangle d_{jb}-\sum_{bj}\langle aj||ib\rangle d_{bj}\]

Take \(f\rightarrow0\) (zero-frequency limit) and rename \(x_{ai}=d_{ai},y_{ai}=d_{ia}\)

\[\left[\begin{array}{cc} A & B\\ B^{*} & A^{*} \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c} X\\ Y \end{array}\right]=\omega\left[\begin{array}{cc} I & 0\\ 0 & -I \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c} X\\ Y \end{array}\right]\]

where

\[A_{ai,bj}=\left(\epsilon_{a}-\epsilon_{i}\right)\delta_{ab}\delta_{ij}+\langle aj||ib\rangle\] \[B_{ai,bj}=\langle ab||ij\rangle\]
entry.summary: There are many different ways to derive the linear response time-dependent HF (LR-TDHF) or LR-TDDFT equation. This derivation is based on the linear response of HF density matrices to an external perturbation following the derivations in the famous paper. The perturbation and the response of density matrices have the same form (same frequency) based on the linear response theory.
